director.chapterArc: A survivalist chapter focusing on the cost of a near-fatal crossing: repairing gear by sacrificing future shelter, correcting a fatigue-induced error in snare-setting through moral grounding with Tonk, harvesting food via 'stealing' from squirrels (the jay), and finally realizing their medical supplies are insufficient for the remaining journey as the fever stabilizes at a dangerous baseline.
director.restraintNote: Maintain Jab's exhausted practicality. The tone is clinical regarding survival tasks but carries an undercurrent of dread during the final arithmetic on medicine. Do not dramatize the 'jay' conversation; it is a lesson in reciprocity, delivered with dry matter-of-factness.

cues.delivery: Internal calculation of resources. Jab's voice is low and measured as he weighs the loss of his brother against the need for shelter repair.
cues.from: He had no spare hide. He had a hide cover, a pack, a pair of boots, a coat, and a brother.
cues.through: He went through it properly, out loud, because thinking it in his head at this hour would have got him a worse answer.
cues.reason: Shift from narrative description to internal monologue regarding survival priorities.

cues.delivery: Gentle physical action. Jab's voice softens as he removes the cover from Tonk and cuts it; a moment of protective tenderness amidst necessity.
cues.through: "That's what it is, then," he said, and got up and slid it gently off Tonk and cut a strip off the short end with the blade lit, drawing it slow to keep the line straight, and put the cover back over him before he had time to get cold. The cover was now four feet by five and a half. In a week he would not remember it had been anything else.
cues.reason: Character focus on protecting the patient during a critical repair.

cues.delivery: Clinical resolution. Jab speaks to himself with finality about the rail's design flaw; a moment of technical acceptance.
cues.from: "That's the answer," he said to it. "The trouble wasn't the length. The trouble was it had a corner."
cues.through: He fell asleep sitting up against the pack with his hand on his brother's chest and woke an hour later with his neck locked, and the fire down, and the sky gone hard and clear and full of stars, and every wet thing in the camp going stiff.
cues.reason: Narrative shift from action to internal realization.

cues.delivery: Realization. Jab's voice is flat and self-critical as he identifies the error in his snare-setting.
cues.through: He knew exactly how it had happened, and it had not happened because he did not know how to set a snare. He had been setting snares since he was six. It had happened because he had set them standing up, in the last of the light, tired to the bone, gauging the height off his own crouch instead of getting his own eye down onto the ground where the hare's eye was — which was what his aunt on the smoking side had made him do for one entire summer, lying on his belly in the willow like an idiot, looking down a trail from a hare's height until he could not unsee it.
cues.reason: Narrative pivot from observation to internal diagnosis.

cues.delivery: Decision. Jab speaks with quiet resolve; the tone is firm but not aggressive.
cues.from: "Morning," he said. "And then we go hard till dark."
cues.through: He reset them from his belly.
cues.reason: Character dialogue establishing a new plan.

cues.delivery: Moral grounding. Jab's voice is conversational and dry as he explains the 'jay' analogy to Tonk; no sentimentality.
cues.reason: Dialogue sequence focusing on ethical instruction.

cues.delivery: Promise. Jab's voice is steady and honest; he acknowledges the lie of his promise while maintaining its truth.
cues.from: "You," said Jab. "When your leg's mended, you're going to walk back up here with a pocket full of something and you're going to do it yourself, and I'll show you the tree."
cues.through: It was not a lie. He had made himself a rule about lies six weeks ago and he had kept it, and this was not one, because he had every intention of it being true and no ability to make it true, and those were two different things.

cues.delivery: Dread. Jab's voice is barely audible as he calculates the medicine shortage; a moment of suppressed panic.
cues.from: "Five days," he said, under his breath. "Five and a half."
cues.reason: Narrative shift to internal realization of impending crisis.

cues.delivery: Confirmation. Jab's voice is flat and detached as he confirms the fever's trajectory.
Resolution. Jab's voice is firm and final as he announces the plan for tomorrow; a shift from observation to action.
cues.through: "Longer than you'll like," Jab said again, and bent to lift him.
cues.reason: Character dialogue establishing the next phase of survival.

pauses.after: He worked on the frame until the middle of the night, which was how he found out what the crossing had actually cost him.
pauses.reason: Completed thought on cost; allows listener to absorb the weight of the crossing's aftermath.

pauses.after: He had no spare hide. He had a hide cover, a pack, a pair of boots, a coat, and a brother.
pauses.reason: Breath group transition from inventory list to decision making.
Emphasis on the scarcity of resources.
Isolating the critical decision point for shelter repair.

pauses.after: It was four feet by six, and he needed a piece three fingers wide and as long as his forearm.
pauses.reason: Completed thought on the specific dimensions; pause before action begins.

pauses.after: "That's the answer," he said to it. "The trouble wasn't the length. The trouble was it had a corner."
pauses.reason: Major realization about the rail's design flaw; needs space for impact.

pauses.after: The loop was a thumb's width above the hair. The whole snare, all four snares, sat a thumb too high.
pauses.reason: Completed thought on the error identification; pause before explanation.
Emphasis on the scale of the error (all four snares).

pauses.after: Four snares. One mistake, repeated four times, because he had made it once and then copied himself.
pauses.reason: Emotional landing of self-recognition regarding fatigue and copying errors.
Isolating the core failure for dramatic weight.
Emphasis on Jab's admission of the 'jay' identity.

pauses.after: It was not a lie. He had made himself a rule about lies six weeks ago and he had kept it, and this was not one, because he had every intention of it being true and no ability to make it true, and those were two different things.
pauses.reason: Major emotional landing on the nature of his promise; a moment of quiet gravity.
Completed thought on inventory count; pause before calculation begins.
Isolating the critical number for dramatic impact.

pauses.after: He sat with that for a while and did not let himself reach the obvious conclusion at speed, because it was the kind of conclusion that would be easier to live with if he had walked all the way around it first. Then he reached it anyway. From tomorrow the morning dose would be half, and the night dose would stay whole, because the nights were where it lived. Half a twist would not hold a morning. He knew that. He had watched what a whole one did to a bad morning and it was not much.
pauses.reason: Pause for the listener to process the grim arithmetic of medicine vs. days remaining.
Emphasis on the grim reality of their timeline.
Isolating the directional confirmation of the fever's rise.
Emphasis on the moment of decision and resolve.

pauses.after: "Nothing." He got his hands under him and stood, and turned his face north, into the wind, where the country climbed one more time before it let go toward the flats and the river and whatever was on the other side of that. "We're going to do a long one tomorrow. Longer than you'll like."
pauses.reason: Major emotional landing on the decision to push harder; sets up the chapter's closing tension.
